setting: A short talk in a music history class about how blues traditions influenced early jazz.
narrator_intro: Listen to part of a talk in a music history class.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Early jazz did not appear from nowhere; it grew out of several African American musical traditions.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: One of the strongest roots is the blues, with its expressive vocal style and flexible pitch.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Blues often uses a twelve-bar structure and “blue notes”—tones bent slightly for emotional color.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: In New Orleans around 1900, brass bands, ragtime rhythms, and blues feeling mixed in dance halls and parades.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Improvisation became central: players invented phrases on the spot while staying within a shared form.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Instruments like the cornet, clarinet, and trombone took turns carrying the melody.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Recording technology later helped jazz travel far beyond its hometown scenes.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Still, many historians say you can hear blues sensibility inside jazz solos even today.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: So when we study jazz history, we listen for those blues DNA strands—not just flashy technique.

talk.speaker: speaker1
talk.text: Next time we’ll compare New Orleans style with the bigger swing bands of the 1930s.

narrator_outro: Now get ready to answer the questions.
